newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS PRESS - FEB 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - BRITISH BUSINESS PRESS - FEB 14.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company.
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- INFLATION TOPS CLARKE TARGET

Figures have been released which suggest Chancellor Kenneth Clarke may be placing too much faith in the strong pound to contain inflation. The new of the "underlying" inflation rate, which excludes mortgages and is target by the government, caused disappointment in the City. Analysts claim the figures were worse than those projected by the Bank of England in a midweek report in which the Bank urged the Chancellor to deliver a "moderate" rise in interest rates.
-- BRITISH BIOTECH CHIEF QUITS

Finance director at British Biotech, James Noble, has resigned, leaving share options worth three million stg. The group is developing a potential treatment for cancer. Chief executive, Keith McCallagh said the departure was amicable and prompted by British Biotech's transition from a drug development operation to a fully fledged pharmaceutical company.
-- REGULATOR DEFENDS BRITISH GAS PROFITS

Clare Spottiswoode, gas industry regulator, has defended British Gas over Labour's plans for a windfall profits tax and rejected suggestions that the company was making too much profit. She says she will tell Shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown that she is ensuring that current profits are reasonable. She also warned that Labour would have to be careful about how it approached the issue in the energy sector because EU legislation would prevent any discrimination.
THE TIMES
-- PEARSON HIT BY 100 MILLION STG PENGUIN DISCOUNT BILL

An American woman employee of Pearson, owner of Penguin, has cost the company 100 million stg in unauthorised discounts since 1991 on book orders given out in exchange for accelerated payments from retailers. Pearson said the discounts, which averaged five per cent, violated company policy and had the effect of boosting the retailers' cash flow at Pearson's expense. Pearson have declined to identify the woman and is investigating the matter.
-- DE SAVARY TO FLOAT NEW 100 MILLION STG VENTURE

Entrepreneur Peter de Savary is planning to float The Carnegie Club, his new venture, with a market value of 100 million stg. The floatation would represent a return to the public arena by de Savary, who lost a large part of his fortune in the 1990s when his Placedon group collapsed, owing 50 million stg. This will be the third time he has run a public company. By the time the company floats it should have a turnover of 40 million stg.
-- TAX CHANGE THREATENS JOBS AND INVESTMENT

The Finance Bill, to be put before Parliament, could put thousands of jobs and hundreds of millions of pounds of investment in major projects at risk. Projects which have relied on lease finance money, which will be put at risk, include the UK plants of Nissan and Toyota, the Trafford Centre development in Manchester and the modernisation of London Underground's Northern Line.
THE GUARDIAN
-- PARTY TARGETS LATE PAYERS

Shadow small business minister Barbara Roche has said, during a Commons debate, that a Labour government would draw up a "league tables" listing the record of large companies in clearing their debts to smaller suppliers to encourage companies to pay their bills promptly. She made it clear that Labour would not be waiting for government to take action on late payment, which she described as the "scourge of small firms".
-- AIRBUS CLAIMS BOEING HAS SUPER-JUMBO UNDER WRAPS

Jean Pierson, managing director of Airbus, a consortium of France's Aerospatiale, Germany's Daimler Benz Aerospace and Spain's Casa, says his group has been warned that Boeing will unveil plans for a super-jumbo ahead of his committment to build a 550-seater jetliner. Airbus will decide whether to build the giant A3XX late next year or in 1999. Airbus aims to break Boeing's monopoly of large-capacity airliner business and win 50 per cent of world market by 2002.
-- FIGHT FOR PART-TIMERS' PENSIONS FAILS

The union representing shop workers, teachers, college lecturers, bank employees and health service staff, the TUC, has lost a two-year battle to win compensation for part-time workers barred from occupational pension schemes in the Court of Appeal. The TUC lodged a number of claims on behalf of several unions after a 1994 ruling in the European Court of Justice that employers who blocked part-timers from pension schemes could be guilty of indirect sex discrimination.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- TALK OF 1.3 BILLION STG BID BY WILLIAMS KEY TO LEAP IN CHUBB SHARES

Williams Holdings is to put in a 1.3 billion stg offer for Chubb, the locks and alarms group, leading to a large jump in Chubb's shares. Analysts say the bid was not unexpected following Chubb's disappointing recent results. Speculation immediately focussed on a handful of potential buyers, including Rentokil Initial, Ingersoll-Rand, Tyco and Republic Industries. One analyst said the sale was another example of chairman Sir Ernest Harrison's focus on creating shareholder value.
-- SFA BARS CROOK FROM UK TRADING

The Serious Fraud Office has banned former senior trader with merchant bank Henry Ansbacher, David Crook, from doing investment business for the "grossly improper" transfer of 70,000 dollars of the banks money to an associate of his in Zimbabwe. He has also been ordered to pay SFA costs of 8,500 stg. An SFA tribunal found that Crook had lied or restored half-truths during interviews with them about his bank accounts.
-- TESCO CUTS NATWEST TIE TO LINK WITH ROYAL BANK

Tesco has announced plans to team up with the Royal Bank of Scotland and sever a five-year financial services partnership with NatWest. NatWest said it had refused to help Tesco expand further into retail banking and insurance. Although Royal Bank has a smaller overlap with Tesco, the supermarket group could soon be competing with NatWest's branches. NatWest may make a claim against Tesco for the cost of pulling out of the five- year contract to manage Tesco Clubcard.
